arguments.issue: Did the Officer unreasonably reject the new evidence under paragraph 113(a) of IRPA?
arguments.claim: The Officer unreasonably dismissed the warrant and colleague's letter without adequate reasons or engagement with the Applicant's affidavit and corroborating evidence.
arguments.quote: The Officer did not say what further proof was needed, and did not engage with the Applicant’s affidavit. The Officer’s one-sentence dismissal of the colleague’s letter as “self-serving” also is not an adequate basis.

support.ref: Raza v Canada, 2007 FCA 385 at para 13
Applicant’s affidavit and news reports at para 3

arguments.weak_spot: The Officer might argue the warrant's authenticity was legitimately doubtful and the letter was unreliable without further proof.

arguments.issue: Did the Officer breach procedural fairness by making credibility findings without a hearing, contrary to paragraph 113(b) of IRPA and section 167 of the IRPR?
arguments.claim: The Officer made a credibility finding by rejecting evidence as unauthenticated without holding a hearing, breaching procedural fairness requirements.
arguments.quote: The Officer here said the warrant “could not be authenticated”, which is, in substance, a finding that the Applicant is not credible. All three of the section 167 factors are met.

support.ref: Singh v Canada, 2016 FCA 96 at paras 49–54

arguments.weak_spot: The Officer may contend that no hearing was required as the evidence was insufficient to raise credibility issues warranting one.

arguments.issue: Did the Officer breach procedural fairness by making credibility findings without a hearing, contrary to paragraph 113(b) of IRPA and section 167 of the IRPR?
arguments.claim: All three factors in section 167 support holding a hearing: serious credibility issue, central evidence, and potential to justify allowing the application.
arguments.quote: All three of the section 167 factors are met.
arguments.weak_spot: The Officer might argue the evidence was not central or did not raise a serious credibility issue.

arguments.issue: Did the Officer properly assess the risk under sections 96 and 97 of IRPA?
arguments.claim: The Officer failed to separately assess the risk tests under sections 96 and 97 and improperly conflated the risk assessment with credibility findings.
arguments.quote: The Officer did not assess either test separately and treated the question as one of credibility.

support.ref: Li v Canada, 2005 FCA 1 at paras 33–34

arguments.weak_spot: The Officer may argue the credibility issues justified the risk assessment approach taken.
